fatal_errors: The proposed CoCrNi short-range-order strategy does not reconstruct the target composition-screening method based on VEC, rule-of-mixtures Young's modulus, and density in Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W alloys.
Atom probe tomography is destructive and cannot straightforwardly provide the claimed in-situ, real-time monitoring and control of SRO during annealing.

The cited evidence supports SRO measurement and strengthening, but not the claimed simultaneous increases in tensile ductility and fracture resistance or the quantitative 15–20% and 10–15% improvements.
Annealing-induced changes in grain size, segregation, precipitation, and texture are not controlled, so an observed property correlation could not be assigned uniquely to SRO.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad structural-alloy objective and proposes a testable processing–structure–property relationship, but it is a different alloy family, intervention, mechanism, baseline, and loading regime from the hidden target. The target screened 38,326 refractory Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W compositions and selected Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 by minimizing VEC while retaining predicted modulus; it then demonstrated room-temperature compressive ductility of 35.7% at 1115 MPa yield strength. The generated proposal instead uses annealing-induced SRO in FCC CoCrNi. Its evidence reasonably supports SRO quantification and increased hardness/strength, while E3 actually warns that SRO can localize strain and cause glide-plane softening, weakening the asserted ductility benefit. Young's-modulus retention is plausible but not an SRO-enabled improvement, and fracture-toughness enhancement is not established by the cited excerpts. A heat-treatment matrix with tensile and toughness testing could discriminate the hypothesis if SRO were measured ex situ and microstructural confounders were controlled, but the stated falsification rule is somewhat circular because the 'optimal window' is undefined and failure could be attributed to not reaching it.
